extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science (philosophers, advanced undergraduates, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: An analytic essay on the notions of causation, scientific law, determinism, and their bearing on free will; it sets out definitions, distinctions, and criteria used to judge when something counts as a law, a cause, a deterministic system, an isolated system, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'same cause, same effect' as a scientific assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional aphorism 'same cause, same effect' is not assumed by science and is 'utterly otiose'; crude uniformities depend on vague event-definitions and are replaced by more differentiated antecedents and consequents as science advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take 'same cause, same effect' as a necessary presupposition of scientific practice; expect scientific explanations to increasingly specify many antecedents (shape, density, latitude, altitude, positions of other bodies) rather than appeal to a simple repeating 'same cause'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic (inductive) criterion for calling A a cause of B
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence A followed by B has been frequently observed and never found to fail, there is an inductive probability that it will continue to hold; in that case the earlier event may be called the 'cause' and the later the 'effect'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an empirical, probabilistic notion of cause: observation-based and fallible (e.g., some matches fail to ignite). It presupposes the inductive principle (treated here as indubitable for argument) and concedes that observed sequences are at best probable, not necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific law as functional/differential relation (sameness of relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific constancy consists not in sameness of causes and effects but in 'sameness of relations' — more precisely, sameness of differential equations: a constant relation between the state of the universe at an instant and the rates of change (e.g., acceleration as a function of configuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer describing laws as mathematical/functional relations (differential equations) that link states and rates of change; this formulation avoids naïve cause/effect talk and better matches how advanced sciences present laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a deterministic system (formal criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system is 'deterministic' when, given certain data [e1,t1,...,en,tn], the state E_t at any time t is a function E_t = f(e1,t1,...,en,tn,t). A system is 'deterministic throughout a given period' if this holds for all t in that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the functional relation (A) as the criterion for determinism and identify the specific determinants (the data) for the system. Note that a system may be deterministic only within a restricted time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants (what counts as determinants of a system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events e1,e2,...,en at specified times are called 'determinants' of the system when they, via the functional relation, determine the state E_t at other times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a system may have many different valid sets of determinants (e.g., configurations of the solar system at two instants determine motion). Determinants need not be unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatively isolated system (criterion for empirical verifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system is 'relatively isolated during a given period' if, within some assignable margin of error, it will behave the same way during that period however the rest of the universe is constituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical verification of a law requires approximate independence from distant conditions; e.g., planetary motions can be treated as if unaffected by distant stars only if those stars are sufficiently remote. One must specify the respect (which variables) in which isolation is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practically isolated system (operational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system is 'practically isolated' during a period if, although in principle there might be states of the rest of the universe causing error beyond the margin, there is reason to believe such states do not in fact occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical isolation in applied contexts (e.g., constructing an almanac) where one assumes no relevant external perturbations up to a given date; this is an empirical, contingent judgment, not a proof of isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verifiability vs. exact (non-verifiable) laws distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two sorts of laws: (1) those empirically verifiable but probably only approximate, and (2) those not empirically verifiable but which may be exact (e.g., the law of universal gravitation may be exact though its empirical application to the solar system is approximate because of distant matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating laws, make explicit whether you mean an approximate, empirically-testable law for a relatively isolated system or a purported exact law of the whole universe; their statuses and evidential bases differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature as inductive principle (limited, not a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'uniformity of nature' (permanence of laws) is accepted on inductive grounds, not a priori; science assumes permanence of particular laws to the degree required by the case (e.g., assume gravitation holds up to year X when making an almanac for year X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat uniformity as probabilistic and context-sensitive: do not elevate it to an absolute major premise; prefer direct induction from observed instances when possible because it yields higher probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as methodological selection, not metaphysical law
rubrics_metrics.description: Science selects the simplest formula that fits the facts; this is a methodological precept, not a law of nature. Many empirically identical past-fitted formulas diverge in the future, so simplicity guides selection but does not make the chosen law necessarily true forever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In model choice and law attribution, justify simplicity as a methodological heuristic, and remain open to replacement when a better-fitting (but perhaps more complex) law is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of absolute time in fundamental laws (heuristic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A helpful principle is that time should not enter explicitly into our fundamental formulæ (laws typically show acceleration as a function of configuration, not of time explicitly); this reduces the problem that arbitrary time-dependent functions could render determinism trivial and vacuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating candidate laws, prefer expressions where time is not an independent argument unless an integrated (lapse-of-time) form legitimately requires it; this constraint helps keep determinism empirically meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for labelling A as cause of B via 'practically isolated system' formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical case where one event A is said to 'cause' another B is the most simplified instance of a practically isolated system: whenever A occurs throughout a period, it is followed by B because A and B form a practically isolated subsystem under general scientific laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calling something a 'cause' is often a pragmatic shorthand for identifying a locally isolated predictive regularity; recognize it as contingent on special circumstances and a matter of empirical luck if it occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: No asymmetry between cause and effect purely from determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent asymmetries (e.g., 'cause determines effect but effect not cause') arise from vague/narrow conceptions of effect vs precise/wide conceptions of cause; depending on definitions one can have plurality of causes or plurality of effects—symmetry is illusory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asserting ontological asymmetry between cause and effect based only on everyday language; analyze the specificity/vagueness of antecedent and consequent definitions when assessing asymmetry claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Causes operate' and spatial/temporal contiguity prejudices rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims such as 'a cause cannot operate when it has ceased to exist' or 'a cause cannot operate except where it is' rest on assimilating causes to volitions and the idea that causes 'operate'; these are prejudices and lead to groundless inferences (e.g., against action at a distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume causes must 'operate' like volitions or be temporally/spatially contiguous to their effects; analyze causal talk in terms of lawful relations rather than anthropomorphic metaphors of operation or compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'mechanical' system (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system is 'mechanical' when it has a set of determinants that are purely material (e.g., positions of matter at times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition when asking whether volitions or mental states are part of materially determined systems; being mechanical does not by itself answer questions about teleology or freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical determination does not settle teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the universe is mechanical (determined by material determinants), this does not determine whether it is teleological: a mechanical system might realize purposes or thwart them; mechanical determination is neutral with respect to teleology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing teleological explanations, do not assume that showing mechanical determinants suffices to deny purposes or final causes; the two questions are logically separable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible multiple kinds of determinants (mental vs material)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system that is susceptible to material determinants may also be susceptible to mental determinants; the same system can be determinable either by sets of material facts or by sets of volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims that mind is 'subject' to matter, consider whether a one-one or many-one relation holds between mind and brain; logical dependence can go either way depending on these relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarified senses of 'necessity' (threefold distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three commonly conflated senses of necessity: ([alpha]) action necessary if performed whatever the agent may wish (determinism does not imply this); ([beta]) propositional function necessary when all its values are true (irrelevant here); ([gamma]) a proposition necessary with respect to a constituent if it is the value of a necessary propositional function (a logical sense applicable to deterministic dependencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinct senses to avoid confusion when discussing whether determinism entails 'necessity' — note that only the logical sense ([gamma]) follows from determinism, and it lacks the emotional significance people often expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'compulsion' and its limits as applied to causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsion is defined: 'Any set of circumstances is said to compel A when A desires to do something which the circumstances prevent, or to abstain from something which the circumstances cause.' This links compulsion to thwarted desire and makes compulsion inapplicable where desire plays no role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of using 'compel' in analyzing natural causation; compulsion presupposes volition and desire and so cannot straightforwardly be applied to non-volitional natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic/ontological distinction about 'determined' futures
rubrics_metrics.description: One sense of 'the future is determined' is merely that it will be what it will be (ontological), which suffices to rebut some anti-determinist arguments; another sense (epistemic) is that we can calculate the future from the past via a formula, which faces difficulties since many indistinguishable past-fitting formulas diverge in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing freedom vs determinism debates, be explicit which sense of determination (ontological vs calculational/epistemic) is being used; many disputes conflate them.
